Transcranial ultrasonic stimulation of the anterior insula will reduce the self-serving attribution bias in a social agency task where participants judge whether outcomes were caused by their own action versus another agent’s action, whereas stimulation of the dorsal anterior cingulate cortex will leave this bias unchanged.

Offline TUS to the anterior insula, but not to the dorsal anterior cingulate cortex, will attenuate participants' tendency to attribute positive outcomes to their own actions in a task that orthogonally manipulates whether outcomes are caused by the participant or by another agent, indicating that the anterior insula's causal role in biased credit assignment extends from non-social Pavlovian learning to social agency judgments.

Temporally targeted online TUS to the anterior insula during feedback presentation will attenuate the Pavlovian learning bias, whereas online TUS to the dorsal anterior cingulate cortex during cue presentation will amplify the persistence bias, indicating that the distinct bias effects depend on the task phase at which each region is engaged.

Transcranial ultrasonic stimulation will produce region-specific changes in excitation-inhibition balance within the anterior insula and dorsal anterior cingulate cortex—measurable as altered glutamate-to-GABA ratios via magnetic resonance spectroscopy—that respectively account for the attenuated Pavlovian learning bias after anterior insula stimulation and the enhanced persistence bias after dorsal anterior cingulate cortex stimulation.
